thyroid-cancer.name: Thyroid cancer
thyroid-cancer.definition: Thyroid cancer is a cancer that starts in the thyroid gland, a gland in the neck that makes hormones.
thyroid-cancer.overview: Early thyroid cancer often causes no symptoms, and the most common sign is a painless lump in the neck that slowly gets bigger. The main types are papillary, follicular, medullary and anaplastic cancer. Surgery is usually the main treatment, and radioactive iodine is often given afterwards. Most people with the common types do well, according to NHS hospital trust information.
causes: The cause of thyroid cancer is often not known
Radiation exposure of the thyroid, particularly in childhood, is a recognised risk factor for differentiated thyroid cancer
Family history can play a part, and other family members may be tested in medullary thyroid cancer
riskFactors: Radiation exposure of the thyroid, especially in childhood
A family history of thyroid cancer or thyroid disease
Age and sex, which affect the risk
signs: A hard, painless lump in the front lower part of the neck that slowly gets bigger
A hoarse voice that lasts more than a few weeks without a clear reason
complications: Spread to nearby lymph nodes, which may be removed during surgery
Return of the cancer after treatment, which is one reason follow-up is arranged
An underactive thyroid after the thyroid is removed, needing lifelong hormone replacement
thyroid-cancer.diagnosis: A GP typically examines the neck, arranges thyroid blood tests and refers the person to a specialist for further tests. A fine needle aspiration biopsy, in which a thin needle removes some cells from the lump, is a key test. An ultrasound scan of the neck helps interpret the biopsy, but it usually cannot show on its own whether a lump is cancer.
thyroid-cancer.treatment: Surgery is usually the main treatment, and depending on the type and stage the whole thyroid or part of it is removed. Radioactive iodine is often given after surgery, because thyroid tissue and most thyroid cancer cells take up iodine. The multidisciplinary team decides whether it is needed. Radiotherapy, targeted medicines and chemotherapy are used in more advanced cases. If the whole thyroid is removed, lifelong thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine is needed.
thyroid-cancer.prevention: The sources reviewed did not describe a proven way to prevent thyroid cancer, and the cause is often not known.
thyroid-cancer.seekCare: A new lump in the neck, a hoarse voice lasting more than a few weeks without a clear reason, or difficulty swallowing or breathing is a reason to see a GP, and Macmillan advises seeing a doctor as soon as possible for a neck lump even if it is painless. If breathing becomes severely difficult, call 999 or go to A&E.

sections.heading: What is thyroid cancer and what types are there?
sections.body:
Thyroid cancer starts in the thyroid gland, which sits in the neck. Doctors group it by how the cancer cells look under a microscope. The main types are papillary, follicular, medullary and anaplastic cancer. Papillary and follicular cancers are the most common, and together they are called differentiated thyroid cancer.

Medullary thyroid cancer is rare. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is very rare and fast growing. The type matters because it shapes the tests and the follow-up that a specialist team recommends. Care is usually planned by a multidisciplinary team of specialists.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of thyroid cancer?
sections.body:
Early thyroid cancer often causes no symptoms at all. The most common sign is a lump in the front, lower part of the neck, which usually feels hard, slowly gets bigger and is not painful. Other possible signs include a hoarse voice that lasts longer than a few weeks without a clear reason, and trouble swallowing or breathing.

Most neck lumps are not cancer, but a lump is still worth having checked. A GP is the first contact for a new lump, a lasting hoarse voice or difficulty swallowing. Macmillan advises seeing a doctor as soon as possible for a lump in the neck, whether or not it is painful. If breathing becomes severely difficult, call 999 or go to A&E.

sections.heading: What causes thyroid cancer and who is at risk?
sections.body:
The cause of thyroid cancer is often not known. Exposure of the thyroid to radiation, particularly in childhood, is described as the most relevant risk factor for differentiated thyroid cancer. A family history of thyroid cancer or thyroid disease is listed in patient guidance as a risk factor. A long-standing goitre, which is an enlarged thyroid, is also named as a risk factor.

Age and sex also affect the risk. For medullary thyroid cancer, other family members may be offered tests to check their own risk. Having a risk factor does not mean that a person will develop thyroid cancer, and many people who develop it have none of these.

sections.heading: How is thyroid cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP typically examines the neck, arranges thyroid blood tests and refers the person to a specialist for further tests. A fine needle aspiration biopsy is a key test. In it, a very thin needle is passed into the thyroid to remove some cells from the lump for examination.

An ultrasound scan of the neck usually cannot show on its own whether a lump is cancer, but it helps in interpreting the biopsy result. The National Cancer Institute says blood tests to check thyroid hormone levels may also be done. Different types of thyroid cancer may be diagnosed with different tests, so the specialist team chooses the tests that suit the situation.

sections.heading: How is thyroid cancer treated?
sections.body:
Surgery is usually the main treatment. Depending on the type and stage, the whole thyroid or part of it is removed, and nearby lymph nodes may also be taken out. Radioactive iodine is often given after surgery. The thyroid gland and most thyroid cancer cells take up iodine, so the radiation acts directly on thyroid tissue and cancer cells.

Whether a person needs radioactive iodine is decided by the multidisciplinary team. Radiotherapy, targeted medicines and chemotherapy are used in more advanced cases. If the whole thyroid is removed, lifelong thyroid hormone replacement is needed, and levothyroxine is the usual long-term medicine.

sections.heading: What happens after treatment and what is the outlook?
sections.body:
After treatment, follow-up is arranged with the specialist team. Follow-up usually combines neck ultrasound with blood tests. For medullary cancer it is similar, but calcitonin is measured rather than thyroglobulin. A patient guide says people with low-risk cancers removed by surgery may not need follow-up care.

Levothyroxine replaces the hormone the thyroid would otherwise make and prevents an underactive thyroid. After cancer treatment, the dose is often set slightly higher than after removal of the thyroid for a non-cancerous reason, with the aim of lowering the chance of the cancer returning. NHS hospital trust information says most people do well, and that the outlook depends on the type of thyroid cancer and how early it is found.

faqs.q: Is every lump in the neck thyroid cancer?
faqs.a: No. Most neck lumps are not cancer. Even so, a new lump is worth having checked, and Macmillan advises seeing a doctor as soon as possible whether or not it hurts. A GP examines the neck and may arrange blood tests and a referral to a specialist.

faqs.q: Does thyroid cancer always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No. Early thyroid cancer often causes no symptoms at all. When symptoms do appear, the most common is a painless lump in the neck that slowly gets bigger. Others include a hoarse voice that does not clear up, and difficulty swallowing or breathing.

faqs.q: Will someone need thyroid hormone tablets after treatment?
faqs.a: If the whole thyroid is removed, lifelong thyroid hormone replacement is needed. Levothyroxine is the usual medicine, and it replaces the hormone the thyroid would otherwise make. After cancer treatment the dose is often set slightly higher than for non-cancerous thyroid removal, with the aim of lowering the chance of the cancer returning.

NHS hospital trust information says most people do well, and many are cured. The outlook depends on the type of thyroid cancer and how early it is found. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is very rare and fast growing, so a specialist team explains the outlook for each person.
